boundary: libpq and the client tools, which allocate from libc and not from a memory context
title: Memory-safety defects in PostgreSQL 17.5's client side, where allocation is a direct libc client
note: The counterpart to backend-175 and mmgr-repros, and the reason it exists: both of those are palloc clients, so every defect in them is nested by construction. PostgreSQL's client side is not -- libpq, psql, pg_dump and fe_utils call malloc, realloc and free directly, about 990 call sites against the backend's 82 -- so a defect here is a libc client and is non-nested. Without this corpus the study has no non-nested arm to compare against, and a mechanism's silence on a nested defect cannot be attributed to the nesting. These cases are C reductions, not SQL: the defect is in the client process and no statement sent to a server can reach it. Each drives the real upstream function with a constructed input, the way mmgr-repros drives the real aset and slab. That also makes them freestanding domains, so unlike backend-175 they need no application VM. All five were reproduced on the host under ASan on 2026-10-06 against shared/corpus.h and shared/driver.c, each driving the real upstream function copied verbatim from the pin (shared/upstream_libpq.c, upstream_pgdump.c, upstream_ecpg.c, upstream_saslprep.c, upstream_bbstreamer.c). Each case's host-asan oracle records the faulting access, its size and the exact size of the region it ran off, so the reduction is checkable against the arithmetic in its live_proof rather than taken on trust. RESULT ON THE PURECAP ARM, 2026-10-06: 3 of 5 detected (00, 02, 04 all SIGPROT with their PG_DEFECT marker printed first), 2 reached-silent (01, 03). Every one of the five verdicts is predicted by one measured fact, and the fact is worth more than the ratio: this guest's malloc rounds capability bounds to a SIZE CLASS, not to the request. Measured requested->granted pairs: 1->16, 4->16, 8->16, 16->16, 24->32, 32->32, 100->112, 400->448, 4096->4096. Lining the cases up against it: 00 writes 4096 bytes into an 8-byte request (cap 16) and faults; 02 walks ~4 GiB from a 1-byte request (cap 16) and faults; 04 reads 24 bytes from offset 24 of a 24-byte request (cap 32) and crosses at offset 32, so it faults; 01 reads offset 400 of a 400-byte request (cap 448) and does not; 03 reads offset 4 of a 4-byte request (cap 16) and does not. So a malloc-granular capability machine sees an overrun exactly when it exceeds the ALLOCATOR'S ROUNDING, not when it exceeds the object. Two of five real CVE-class defects are invisible here for that reason alone, with no nesting involved at all -- which is a second blind spot, independent of the one this corpus was built to measure, and it narrows the claim that non-nested defects are the ones such a mechanism catches. On fault attribution: these cases cannot use mmgr-repros' .globl label on the faulting instruction, because in three of the five that instruction is inside a function copied verbatim from upstream and a label would make the copy no longer verbatim. The handler in shared/driver.c reports the faulting PC and the return address as offsets from a function the case names instead, which attributes the fault without touching upstream code; case 00 is why both are reported, since its fault is inside libc's memcpy and only the return address lands in pqGetnchar. One field is NOT usable here and is recorded so nobody relies on it: on this guest SIGPROT arrives with si_addr equal to the faulting PC, not to the data address -- measured as addr==pc on all three faulting cases -- so the fault address cannot be cross-checked against an object's bounds from siginfo.
